blocks.text: The hen sometimes lays its egg on dung heaps, but never on a sloping spot where it could easily roll down and be broken (Sabbat 42b). At first the egg hangs on the stalk, but detaches itself once it has acquired its shell (Temura 31a). The egg requires 10 days for its formation and 21 days of brooding (Bechoroth 8a; on Rashi's erroneous explanation of this passage cf. §. 17). The egg that is taken out of a slaughtered hen after its death, as well as the egg that the hen conceives by lying in sun-warmed sand, [p. 197] are not capable of being hatched (§. 183). According to Aristotle (Thierg. 6, 2, 6), however, wind-eggs can still be made fertile if the hen, during the time in which the yolk has not yet been changed into the white, is still fertilized by a bird of the other sex*).

The eggs resulting from being trodden by the cock the hen lays only by day, whereas the wind-eggs also at night (Beza 7a). Treading takes place among fowl only by day (ibid.). The hen refrains from lying down in warm sand if a cock is near her, or at least so near that she can hear his crowing by day (when the echo of sound does not carry as far as at night) (ibid.). The hen then seeks out the cock, and if there is a river between her and the cock, she crosses the bridge, which she refrains from doing only if the crossing is attended with danger (ibid.). The hen sometimes abandons eggs on which she has already begun to brood, and one must then bring her back if the eggs are not to spoil; one can, however, also let another hen continue brooding the eggs (Pesachim 55b). In general, the fowl sometimes leave their dwelling and settle in gardens (Chulin 138b). A proper nest, however, the heavy birds do not, as is well known, build for themselves. The time of egg-laying is not always the same; as a rule the hen lays every other day (see in detail (Nidda 39b).

Fowl are very lustful, and the cock never goes far from the hens (Berachoth 22a). He courts the hens before he treads them (Erubin 100b). The extraordinary fertility of fowl (17 hens on a parsonage farm in the year 1821 laid no fewer than 3568 eggs, thus on average 209 eggs per hen; Voigt l. c. 2. p. 43) gave rise to the custom of carrying a pair of fowl before a bridal couple on their wedding day (Gittin 57a). Hen's eggs are cooked through the most quickly (Sabbat 80b, which admittedly refers to the eggs of large birds, such as ducks, geese etc.). The cock is, among [p. 198] the birds, the most wanton and is very hardy (iy, Rashi: אנדריש, endurci, Beza 25b); he is quarrelsome and inclined to bite against other cocks (Pesachim 113b), and particularly notorious in this respect were the cocks from the house of Bakia; they tolerated no intruders in their midst (Jebamoth 84a). Once a cock killed a child by pecking at its skull with its beak (Berachoth 27a).

Hen droppings (whose smell varies, see p. 55, note*) are dangerous for cattle and animals if they eat them (Chulin 58b); yet they are used for medicinal purposes (Gittin 69b, but erroneously, since a different bird is meant there, see §. 255).

Another use of the hen in medicine was that one who is bitten by a snake on a limb puts that limb into a hen torn apart alive, whereby the poison is drawn out (Joma 83b). Peculiar was the use of fowl for threshing (B. mez. 91b).

The best among poultry is a hen that stays among wine presses and, through feeding on grape skins, sometimes becomes so fat that it cannot step over a reed lying in its way (B. mez. 86b). Fowl like to eat vetch (Terumoth 11, 9); they also scratch on dung heaps and consume insects and worms, which they swallow alive (Kelim, 8, 5); for this reason fowl were not kept in Jerusalem, because they might scratch up defiling objects (B. Kama 82b). Although the hen, while scratching on dung heaps, remains unmolested by the weasels living there (Pesachim 8b), one nevertheless had to make the air holes in the hen coops so small that weasels could not get in through them (Sabbat 146a and b).

White fowl were preferably chosen for pagan sacrifices (A. Sara 13b; cf. on this Or. Chajim §. 605), and the cock served superstition as an omen at the conclusion of a business transaction (Horajoth 12a). Finally it may be mentioned that the blood of the hen has different colors; that which streams out of the neck veins is red, that in the limbs is darker, i.e. blackish-red, and that in the entrails is saffron-yellow (§. 80). The following Midrash passage (Rabba Wajikra fol. 193, d) may also find its place here; it reads: “As long as the chicks are young, the mother hides them under her wings, warms them and gathers food for them; but as soon as they have grown up and one of them still wants to cling to its mother, [p. 199] she pecks it on the head and says to it: ““Scratch on your own dung heap!""
Given the numerous species of the dove genus
more than a hundred of them are counted

it is necessary from the outset to name the species mentioned in the Talmud, though some species cannot be determined with apodictic certainty. In all there are ten species, namely a) the domestic pigeon, of which three varieties occur, b) the turtledove in three varieties, c) the veiled pigeon, d) the tumbler pigeon, and e) the wild pigeon in two varieties.
Generic names for dove are: יונה (Berachoth 53b); the young dove: בן יונה (Chulin 22a, usually occurring in the pl. בני יונים) and בר גוזלא (ibid. 76b).
